claim: George Daniels worked at Chess Records, then at a Black-owned record wholesale company on Michigan Avenue.
Daniels managed a wholesale record shop in 1968 and assumed ownership in 1969, renaming it George's Music Room.
George's Music Room became an in-store promotional stop for recording artists.

Daniels founded the National United Independent Retailers, an organization dedicated to protecting African American-owned independent retailers; the HistoryMakers finding aid dates the founding to 1990.
HistoryMakers characterizes George's Music Room as benefiting surrounding North Lawndale businesses and as a site where Daniels mentored neighborhood youth.
Bob Koester founded Delmark Records in 1953 (originally 'Delmar') and relocated the label to Chicago in 1958.
In 1959 Koester took over Seymour's Jazz Mart at 439 S. Wabash Ave. from songwriter Seymour Schwartz and renamed it Jazz Record Mart.
Delmark Records was subsidized by the store's sales, giving Koester freedom to record and curate across genres.
Jazz Record Mart's final address was 27 E. Illinois St.; the store closed in 2016, with Koester attributing the closure to rising rent.
Calkins (2019) finds that between 1980 and 1990, record stores outside majority-white areas had significantly higher failure probabilities than stores within majority-white areas.
Calkins (2019) finds record stores were once more clustered in predominantly Black areas than they were by 2010.
Davis (2011) reports that close to 1,000 African American-owned record stores operated in the South during their heyday.

Davis (2011) documents that Black store owners often had difficulty securing supplier credit and had to pay cash for inventory — a supply-side constraint, not evidence of stores extending credit to customers.
Vee-Jay Records was founded in 1953 by Vivian Carter and James Bracken, who owned a record store in Gary, Indiana; Carter was also a DJ.

Russell Lee photographed the corner of Maxwell and Halsted Streets, Chicago, in April 1941; the image sits in the Library of Congress Prints & Photographs Division, FSA-OWI Collection, reproduction number LC-USF33-012984-M5.
George's Music Room stood at 3915 W. Roosevelt Road in North Lawndale.

Imports Etc., on a side street in Chicago's Printers Row, was in 1986 the city's only record store dealing exclusively in dance music; most of its customers were DJs, stocking new 12-inch singles, old Philadelphia soul, and Italian imports.
After Farley 'Jackmaster' Funk played Telex's 'Brainwash' (Belgian group, English lyrics by Sparks) in his sets, Imports Etc. sold 1,000 copies in two weeks.

Chip E. worked at Imports Etc.; after local DJs played his acetate of 'Like This,' he pressed 1,000 copies (borrowing his mother's income-tax check), sold 500 the first day and the rest within the week.
The WBMX Hot Mix 5 created record demand before release: DJs brought rough mixes to the show, and exposure ensured enough profit to fund the next pressing.
Gramaphone Records opened in 1969.
Joe Dale and Carl Borowski took over Gramaphone in 1978, and the store shifted toward dance music in the early 1980s.

Gramaphone employed working DJs — including Derrick Carter, Ralphi Rosario, DJ Sneak, DJ Heather, DJ Colette, Mark Farina, and Jesse De La Peña — functioning as a retail library, peer-learning environment, equipment-advice point, and professional pipeline.
Vivian Carter played records for teenagers in her Gary, Indiana record store, solicited their reactions, and used that feedback in talent and record decisions — a store-as-A&R case.
Before computerized reporting, Billboard's charts drew separately on self-reported record-store sales, DJ playlists, and jukebox plays.
More than 20 Black-owned stores formed the F.A.M.S. Coalition (Forever a Music Store) in 2021, seeking industry support, exclusives, vinyl variants, release parties, and equal opportunity.
Warner executive Steve Corbin described Black independent stores as important in breaking records in the early 1990s.
In the Ticketron/Ticketmaster era, concert tickets were commonly bought at record stores; fans lined up outside record stores for tickets.
Ora Nelle (Maxwell Radio) sold discs from a Maxwell Street storefront.
Jukebox operators tracked plays by location and regularly changed selections; Black and working-class artists often reached listeners through jukeboxes despite limited radio access.
By 1954, Midwest jukebox operators were receiving rising requests for R&B in teenage locations.
A 1970s Billboard piece documents Black entrepreneurs' barriers in one-stop/wholesale operations, including Jerry Augustus's Hitsville co-op one-stop in New York.
Charles L. Hughes (Country Soul, 2015): country-soul-era record stores sold records but also other goods; staff listened to customer requests; stores were sites of 'musical cross-pollination.'
Gramaphone Records is located at 2843 N. Clark St.; Hyde Park Records at 1377 E. 53rd St.
Joe Dale died in March 2025 (announced March 26, 2025); Gramaphone's statement called him an 'unsung hero of house music.'
In the Sway's Universe interview, George Daniels describes how labels' distribution and pricing practices undercut Black-owned mom-and-pop stores.
Gramaphone Records was featured in the documentary Better Living Through Circuitry.
Gramaphone was 'the first of its kind in the Chicago area, focusing on vinyl for DJs.'
Koester ran Jazz Record Mart for nearly 50 years at multiple Chicago locations before opening Bob's Blues & Jazz Mart in Irving Park in 2016; he sold Delmark to Julia A. Miller in 2018.
George's Music Room's closure date: TRiiBE/sibling reporting says 2010; an IMDb documentary description says 2017.
Imports Etc. owner surname: 'Weisburg' in some accounts, 'Weisberg' in others; store name rendered 'Importes, Etc.' and 'Imports Etc.'
The origin of the name 'house music': store bin labeling is one participant account among several (Knuckles's Warehouse vs. Farley's 'nobody in the city was playing imports' account in SPIN 1986).
A 1979 record pool operated at Imports Etc.
DJ Ron Hardy used Imports Etc. as a supply base.
Koester's store directly incubated Alligator Records, Living Blues magazine, and Flying Fish Records.

claim: Roland Corporation (founder Ikutaro Kakehashi; engineers Tadao Kikumoto, Makoto Muroi, Hiro Nakamura, Hisanori Matsuoka) invented the TR-808, TB-303, and TR-909 for other purposes; Chicago's Black producers and DJs culturally transformed them — they did not invent them.
notes: Load-bearing thesis; exact formulation required by brief standards.

claim: The Roland TR-808 Rhythm Composer (1980-1983) was fully analog, one of the first programmable drum machines (step sequencing, accents, DIN sync); list price US$1,195; fewer than 12,000 units sold; a commercial failure against the sample-based Linn LM-1.
The TR-808 design team was led by chief engineer Tadao Kikumoto; Makoto Muroi was a chief engineer; Hiro Nakamura designed the voice circuits; Hisanori Matsuoka developed the software and hardware.

The Roland TB-303 Bass Line (1981-1984) was designed by Tadao Kikumoto, marketed as a 'computerised bass machine' to replace the bass guitar; it was monophonic analog subtractive with a 24 dB/octave resonant low-pass filter and built-in step sequencer; it failed commercially and was discontinued after a small production run.

The Roland TR-909 Rhythm Composer (1983) was designed by Tadao Kikumoto; it combined analog drum voices (kick, snare, toms, clap) with digitally sampled cymbals and hi-hats, and was Roland's first MIDI-equipped drum machine; it was a commercial failure (~10,000 units, production ended after about a year) as buyers preferred fully sample-based machines.

The Technics SL-1200 direct-drive turntable was released in October 1972 by Matsushita Electric under the Technics brand, developed in 1971 by a team led by engineer Shuichi Obata; high-torque direct drive enabled slip-cueing and backward cueing impossible on belt drives; more than 3 million units were sold; an SL-1210MK2 is displayed at the London Science Museum as a world-changing technology.

Phuture created 'Acid Tracks' in 1985 around a secondhand Roland TB-303; Ron Hardy club-tested it from cassette at the Music Box in 1985; it was officially pressed on Trax Records in 1987. First-created 1985; first-club-tested 1985; first-pressed 1987.
notes: Chronology corroborated across MusicRadar, Roland articles, and Wikipedia. Real-time filter-knob manipulation while patterns ran is the documented technique.

claim: 'On & On' (Jesse Saunders, written/produced with Vince Lawrence) was recorded in 1983 on a Tascam 4-track using a Roland TR-808, Korg Poly-61, and Roland TB-303, and released on Jes Say Records in early 1984; it is defensible only as the first house track committed to vinyl.
notes: Qualified 'first' per CTL-DR-MUSIC-001 standing rule.

claim: Before producing original tracks, Frankie Knuckles cut and spliced disco and pop records on a quarter-inch Pioneer reel-to-reel machine (late 1970s/early 1980s); he described reassembling tape fragments 'no more than half a second of sound' with millisecond-level rhythmic precision, citing his edit of Michael Jackson's 'Thriller'.
notes: Direct practitioner quotes from the 2012 MusicRadar interview.

claim: In the mid-1980s at the Power Plant, Frankie Knuckles wired the Roland TR-909 he obtained from Derrick May directly into his DJ mixer and ran it underneath every record that night: 'every record I played that night had a 909 running underneath it'.

claim: Larry Heard identified a Roland Jupiter-6 as the instrument for the 'Can You Feel It' bassline and chords: 'it's not like a stock sound... it was more a case of experimenting and turning the knobs when everything was running'.
notes: Direct practitioner quote, Deep House Amsterdam interview.

claim: Larry Sherman, a vintage-jukebox collector, bought the Musical Products pressing plant in Chicago's Bridgeport neighborhood in 1983 and began pressing records; Trax Records was launched from that plant base in 1984-85 and released 'No Way Back' (1986), 'Can You Feel It' (1986), 'Your Love' (1988), 'Move Your Body' (1986), and 'Acid Tracks' (1987); in 1991 Trax declared bankruptcy when distributors owing it $4.5 million went out of business.

The Hot Mix 5 (Farley Keith, Mickey Oliver, Ralphi Rosario, Kenny Jason, Scott Silz) were assembled by WBMX program director Lee Michaels in 1981 for 'Saturday Night Live, Ain't No Jive' on 102.7 FM; the show reached #1 in Chicago radio ratings with over 2 million listeners.
Ikutaro Kakehashi founded the Roland Corporation in Osaka in 1972 and won a Technical Grammy for MIDI development in 2013.
Marshall Jefferson recorded piano and bass parts for 'Move Your Body' slowly and sped the tape up to final tempo (speed manipulation as a production technique).
notes: Technique is corroborated; exact tempo figures are PROVISIONAL (C-034).

claim: DJ Pierre bought his TB-303 secondhand for about $40: 'somebody took it to a secondhand store, and they put a $40 price tag on it'.
notes: The quote is VERIFIED; the price as a market fact is SUPPORTED (single-source quote).

claim: Jesse Saunders used the Roland TR-808 on 'On & On' 'simply because it was the only drum machine [he] had access to'.
By the mid-1980s, used TR-808s could sell for around US$100 as the failed machines flooded the secondhand market.

TR-808 production ended in 1983 in part because faulty transistors essential to its noise circuit could no longer be restocked after semiconductor improvements; Roland had deliberately bought faulty transistors for their sizzle.
notes: Engineering-history account (EEJournal), consistent with Wikipedia; single detailed source.

claim: Marshall Jefferson, then doing A&R at Trax, agreed to mix 'Acid Tracks' and had Phuture slow it from ~130 BPM to ~120 BPM before the 1987 pressing.

Ron Hardy first played Phuture's 'Acid Tracks' cassette at the Music Box in 1985; the floor emptied on first play and the track won the crowd over after repeated plays the same night; it was then bootlegged on microcassette and sometimes misattributed to Hardy himself.
notes: Roland's article is the detailed source; promotional interest noted.

claim: Ron Hardy's early DJ setup (Den One, 1974) centered on two turntables, a mixer, and a reel-to-reel tape deck.

claim: In 1985 Marshall Jefferson bought a sequencer plus a keyboard, drum machine, and mixer for around $9,000 on credit from his post-office job, and wrote his first song two days later; that rig was used to make 'Move Your Body'.
